planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright light to full sun in fast-draining, gritty cactus mix; Sea Urchin Cactus is one of the more forgiving and variable Gymnocalycium species for beginners.

directions: Grow in bright light to full sun in fast-draining, gritty cactus-and-succulent mix, watering thoroughly then letting the soil dry completely before watering again. This variable Argentine species forms an egg-shaped to globular, gray-green body with prominent, sharply gibbous ribs bearing stout, straight to slightly curved spines that range from pale horn to dark brown depending on the individual plant. Funnel-shaped white to soft pink flowers open from the crown in late spring and early summer, often appearing on plants still just a few inches across. Reduce water sharply through the cool winter months to prevent rot and to encourage the following season's bloom.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America reference

planting.note: Plant offsets or nursery starts in spring into very well-drained, gritty soil in bright light with some midday shade; this is among the smallest and cold-hardiest chin cacti and clusters readily into a mat.

directions: Plant in very well-drained, gritty soil in bright light with light shade from the harshest afternoon sun, watering only after the mix has dried fully. Tiny, flattened, gray-green globes with fine, comb-like spines cluster and offset rapidly from the base, quickly forming a dense mound of small heads. In spring it produces an abundance of pale pink to white flowers so numerous they can nearly hide the plant body, opening readily even on offsets barely an inch across. Native to high-elevation sites in Argentina, it tolerates cooler nights and brief light frost better than most globular cacti, but still needs a dry, frost-free winter rest indoors or under cover in colder climates.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America
San Diego Cactus and Succulent Society

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright light to full morning sun in fast-draining, mineral-rich cactus mix; the flattened body scorches in intense unshaded summer sun.

directions: Grow in bright, filtered light or morning sun with afternoon shade in fast-draining, gritty cactus mix, watering only once the soil has dried completely. The flattened, gray-green to purplish-bronze globe has low, sharply notched ribs and short, pale, backward-curving spines pressed close to the body. Large white flowers with a distinctive dark red throat open from the crown in late spring, strikingly wide relative to the small plant body. Give it a cool, dry winter rest and increase water gradually as new growth resumes in spring to encourage the best flowering.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America reference

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright light to full sun in fast-draining cactus mix; Crown Cactus flowers most reliably after a cool, dry winter rest followed by a spring increase in water.

directions: Grow in bright light to full sun in fast-draining cactus mix, watering thoroughly and then allowing the soil to dry out completely before the next watering. The rounded, blue-green stem is distinctively marked with white, comb-like areoles running in neat rows along each rib, giving the body a frosted, silvery look that contrasts sharply with a ring of vivid orange-red flowers that circle the crown in spring. It clusters and offsets freely at the base over time, forming an attractive colony in a shallow pot. Native to high-elevation sites in Bolivia, it tolerates cooler nights well but should be kept dry and frost-free through winter to set the next season's flower buds.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America reference

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright light to full sun in fast-draining cactus mix; give a cool, dry winter rest to trigger the heaviest spring bloom.

directions: Grow in bright light to full sun in fast-draining cactus mix, watering thoroughly and then letting the mix dry out fully before watering again. Small, soft-looking globular stems are covered in fine, hair-like golden to reddish-brown spines that give the whole plant a fuzzy, bristling texture, and it clusters readily into a low mound of offsets. In spring, bright orange to orange-red flowers open in a ring around the upper stems, often produced in such quantity that they nearly obscure the plant. Keep it dry and frost-free through winter, and separate rooted offsets in spring to start new clusters.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America
San Diego Cactus and Succulent Society

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright light to full sun in fast-draining cactus mix; the blue-gray body color is most vivid under strong light.

directions: Grow in bright light to full sun in fast-draining cactus mix, watering deeply and then letting the soil dry out completely between waterings. The strongly ribbed, blue-gray to steel-blue globe is edged with short golden-yellow spines along each rib, and clusters over time into a tight group of offsets around the original stem. Clear yellow, cup-shaped flowers open from the crown in early summer, contrasting sharply with the cool-toned body. Native to grassy hillsides in southern Brazil and Uruguay, it tolerates brief cool spells better than many desert cacti but should be kept dry and frost-free in winter.

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright light to full sun in fast-draining cactus mix; the dense white spination is most attractive with strong, even light.

directions: Grow in bright light to full sun in fast-draining cactus mix, watering thoroughly and letting the soil dry completely before the next watering. Slender, cylindrical to globular stems are so densely covered in fine white radial spines and longer bristly central spines that the green body beneath is almost entirely hidden, giving the plant an overall silvery-white appearance. Bright yellow, occasionally reddish-tinged flowers open near the crown in summer, opening only a few at a time over an extended season. It slowly elongates from a ball into a short column with age and benefits from a dry, cool winter rest to keep the spination tight and prevent stretching.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America reference

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright light to full sun in fast-draining cactus mix; Scarlet Ball Cactus is valued for flowering unusually early, often in late winter.

directions: Grow in bright light to full sun in fast-draining cactus mix, watering deeply and then allowing the mix to dry out fully before watering again. The flattened to globular stem is densely covered in short, white to pale gray spines that give the whole plant a soft, snowy appearance, over which clusters of brilliant scarlet-red flowers open at the crown in late winter to early spring, notably earlier in the season than most other globular cacti. It remains compact for many years and rarely needs repotting into a much larger container. Provide a cool, dry rest in winter to encourage the earliest and heaviest bloom, then resume normal watering as flower buds appear.

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright light to full sun in fast-draining cactus mix; Silver Cluster Cactus offsets so freely it quickly fills out a shallow pot.

directions: Grow in bright light to full sun in fast-draining cactus mix, watering thoroughly and letting the soil dry out completely before watering again. Small, cylindrical to globular heads are covered in fine, golden-white bristly spines and multiply rapidly by offsetting, soon forming a dense mounded cluster of dozens of heads in a single pot. Small creamy-yellow to pale orange flowers appear around the tips of the offsets in late spring, followed by bright red, club-shaped fruits that persist for weeks and add a second season of color. Because it clusters so vigorously, divide and repot congested clumps every few years to keep the colony healthy and well aerated.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America reference

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright light to full sun in fast-draining cactus mix; the unusually large, soft tubercles are prone to rot if watered too often.

directions: Grow in bright light to full sun in fast-draining, gritty cactus mix, watering deeply and then allowing the soil to dry out completely before the next watering. The stem is made up of unusually large, soft, finger-like tubercles rather than the tight, small nipples typical of most Mammillaria species, giving the plant a loose, spidery silhouette, each tipped with a small cluster of thin spines. Large, funnel-shaped, clear yellow flowers open from among the tubercles in late spring, disproportionately showy for the size of the plant. It offsets slowly at the base over time to form a small clump and is best kept in a shallow, wide pot to accommodate its spreading, finger-like growth habit.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America reference
